analysis|02-18|1930|Ανακαλύπτεται ο Πλούτωνας|Pluto is discovered|In the early twentieth century astronomers suspected that there was another planet beyond Neptune, because of small deviations in the orbits of the outer planets. The search was methodical, with photographic plates compared with one another to detect moving bodies. The effort required patience and precise observation. // On 18 February 1930 the astronomer Clyde Tombaugh, at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona, discovered an object moving across the sky, which was later named Pluto. The discovery was widely announced and regarded as a major scientific achievement. Tombaugh had worked for years on the study of photographic plates. // For decades Pluto was regarded as the ninth planet of the solar system, until in 2006 the International Astronomical Union classified it among the dwarf planets. Its discovery opened the way to the study of the objects of the Kuiper Belt. Its history shows how scientific classification changes as new data accumulate. The discovery fuelled the debate about the boundaries and properties of planets. It contributed to widening knowledge of the limits of the solar system and of the properties of distant bodies, and it allowed astronomers to observe the region beyond Neptune in new ways.

analysis|02-18|1932|Ιδρύεται το κράτος του Μαντσουκούο|The state of Manchukuo is founded|In the early 1930s Manchuria, in northern China, was an area of major Japanese economic presence, especially in railways and mines. Japan sought control of the region for raw materials and for strategic security. Tensions with the Chinese government were intense after the incident of 1931. // On 18 February 1932 the Japanese administration declared the independence of Manchuria from China, and the new state was named Manchukuo. The declaration was made under Japanese influence, with a government that in practice operated under Japanese control. The international community did not widely recognise the declaration. // The creation of Manchukuo became one of the causes of international outrage and of Japan's withdrawal from the League of Nations. The region later became a base for Japanese expansion in Asia. The history of the state is today discussed as an example of the conflict over sovereignty in the region. The declaration is a critical chapter for understanding the causes of the Second World War in Asia. The creation of the state was part of Japan's broader strategy in Asia during this period. The administration of the new state relied on Japanese officials, a fact that was hotly debated in the international arena.

analysis|02-18|1943|Συλλαμβάνονται τα μέλη του «Λευκού Ρόδου»|Members of the White Rose are arrested|During the Second World War Nazi Germany had imposed a strict regime of control, and resistance was limited and dangerous. The group "White Rose" consisted of students from Munich, who wrote and distributed leaflets against the regime. Their activity included texts calling for moral resistance. // On 18 February 1943 the siblings Scholl, Sophie and Hans, were arrested by the Gestapo, after they had distributed leaflets at the university. The arrest followed the discovery of their activity and was the first step towards the trial and execution of the members of the group. The news shocked the student circles of the city. // The activity of the White Rose has remained in history as a symbol of moral resistance against totalitarianism. The figures of the students are today honoured in Germany with monuments and educational activities. Their example is discussed as evidence that individual responsibility can stand against authority. Their memory remains a key element of the German debate about democracy. The memory of this group is taught today as an example of moral resistance under conditions of oppression. These students remain today a model for young people who resist injustice by peaceful means.

analysis|02-18|1965|Η Γκάμπια γίνεται ανεξάρτητη|The Gambia becomes independent|The Gambia is a small country in West Africa that for a long period was under British rule, with an economy based mainly on agriculture and trade. In the years after the Second World War political parties emerged that demanded self-government. The transition to independence took place gradually, through elections and constitutional arrangements. // On 18 February 1965 the Gambia became an independent state and continued to take part in the Commonwealth of Nations. The transition took place peacefully, with the local leader taking over the post of prime minister. Independence was regarded as an important step for the national identity of the country. // Independence opened the way to building democratic institutions, although the country later faced political difficulties. The Gambia continued its trade relations with Britain and with the neighbouring countries of the region. Its history shows the challenges faced by small African states after colonialism. The day is still celebrated as a national anniversary. The national identity of the country took shape gradually after independence, with new institutional structures and with dialogue among the political forces. The country continued to cooperate with its neighbours, and the region became a field of joint initiatives for development.

analysis|02-19|1473|Γεννιέται ο αστρονόμος Νικόλαος Κοπέρνικος|The astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus is born|In the mid-fifteenth century Europe stood at the beginning of a great intellectual upheaval, with the growth of universities and of mathematics. Poland was a powerful kingdom with important centres of learning. The science of astronomy rested on the geocentric system of Ptolemy, which was regarded as beyond question. // On 19 February 1473 Copernicus was born in Toruń in Poland, into a merchant family. He studied in Kraków and at Italian universities, where he worked on mathematics, astronomy and medicine. Later he developed the idea that the Earth and the other planets move around the Sun. // Copernicus's theory, which was published shortly before his death, profoundly changed the way humanity understands the universe. The idea became the starting point of the scientific revolution, and it influenced Galileo, Kepler and Newton. His figure is today linked with the fundamental change in the way of thinking about the world. His story is a point of reference for every discussion of scientific change. His theory was the starting point for a broader debate on how science overturns old certainties. The combination of observation and mathematical calculation became the model for modern astronomy.

analysis|02-19|1878|Ο Έντισον παίρνει δίπλωμα για τον φωνογράφο|Edison receives a patent for the phonograph|At the end of the nineteenth century sound recording was still unknown as a technology, and recording the human voice was regarded as a challenge for engineers. Thomas Edison, who had already gained fame through his inventions in electricity, worked on many experiments to transmit and record sound. The market was waiting for new devices that would change entertainment and business communication. // In February 1878 Edison received a patent for the phonograph, a device that could record and reproduce sound on a cylinder. The device worked with a needle that engraved the vibrations onto a sheet of tinfoil, and the same process was reversed for playback. The invention was presented publicly and aroused great interest. // The phonograph opened the way to the recording industry and to the mass dissemination of music. Later improvements, such as discs, made the device more practical and commercial. The history of the invention is linked with the birth of modern entertainment, and it is regarded as a milestone in the history of the media. Today sound recording is a basic element of our daily lives. The invention was widely discussed in the press of the time, and the device became a symbol of the technical creativity of the century. Edison went on improving the phonograph in the following years.

analysis|02-19|1915|Αρχίζει η ναυτική επίθεση στα Δαρδανέλια|The naval attack on the Dardanelles begins|At the beginning of the First World War the Ottoman Empire had allied itself with the Central Powers, and Britain and France were looking for a way to open a new front. The Dardanelles, the strait that connects the Aegean with the Sea of Marmara, was a strategic point for controlling access to Constantinople. The operation was designed as a naval pressure to force Turkey out of the war. // On 19 February 1915 British and French ships began to bombard the Ottoman forts at the entrance to the Dardanelles. The first blows had limited effect, since the forts were strong and the minefields made the passage of the ships difficult. The attack prepared the ground for the larger campaign that followed. // The operation at the Dardanelles ended in failure, and the troops that landed later at Gallipoli suffered heavy losses. The campaign left deep marks on discussions about the strategy of the war and about the responsibilities of the commands. For the peoples of the region, the Dardanelles remain a symbol of the conflict that shaped the era. This campaign was one of the most ambitious operations of the war's first year, and the losses that followed teach today about the limits of naval power. The study of the failure continues in military academies.

analysis|02-19|1942|Το διάταγμα 9066 του Ρούζβελτ|Roosevelt's Executive Order 9066|After the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 the United States found itself at war with Japan, and the government feared that some citizens of Japanese descent might cooperate with the enemy. This concern was reinforced by the climate of racial prejudice of the time. The authorities demanded security measures for the coastal areas of the western part of the country. // On 19 February 1942 President Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, which allowed Americans of Japanese descent to be confined in camps. Thousands of people, many of whom were American citizens, were moved from their homes to isolated areas with restricted freedoms. The decision was based on military arguments, but it was not accompanied by individual proof of guilt. // The order is today regarded as one of the darkest pages of American history. In 1988 Congress apologised and provided for compensation to the victims. The case is used as an example of the dangers of racial discrimination in times of crisis and of the need to protect individual rights. This large-scale operation affected the lives of thousands of families, who lost their property and their social position. The matter remains to this day a point of reference in the debate on equality and rights.

analysis|02-19|1942|Η ιαπωνική επίθεση στο Ντάργουιν|The Japanese attack on Darwin|At the beginning of 1942 Japan had conquered a large part of Southeast Asia and was pushing the war towards the south. Northern Australia, and in particular the city of Darwin, was regarded as strategically important for the link with the Pacific islands. The area had limited defences, and the Australian government was worried about a possible invasion. // On 19 February 1942 Japanese aircraft bombed Darwin, with almost 250 planes in an operation that lasted a few hours. The strikes destroyed the port, ships and installations, and caused many deaths. The attack was the first and largest Japanese attack on Australian soil. // The event showed that the war had reached the limits of Australia and prompted the government to strengthen the defences and to closer cooperation with the United States. The attack remains an important chapter in the Australian history of the Second World War. Its memory is still discussed as a lesson on the security of coastal cities. The incident heightened the sense of vulnerability in Australia and contributed to the reorganisation of the defence of the northern coast. The battles of the period are discussed as an example of the strategic pressure of the war. This history is also linked with the memory of the local residents, who lived for months in fear of new attacks and with limited means of protection.

analysis|02-19|1945|Η μάχη της Ιβο Τζίμα|The Battle of Iwo Jima|At the end of the Second World War the Americans were advancing their military presence towards Japan, and Iwo Jima, a small volcanic island south of Tokyo, was of strategic importance. The island had airfields and fortifications that could be used for counter-attacks. The Japanese garrison was well fortified in underground positions. // On 19 February 1945 American marines landed on the island, in an operation regarded as one of the hardest in the Pacific. The battles lasted more than a month, with heavy losses on both sides. The Japanese resisted at every position, and the fighting took place in narrow passages, caves and pillboxes. // The capture of the island gave the United States an air base that was used for the bombing of Japan. The battle has remained in history as a symbol of the cruelty of war in the Pacific. The losses and the endurance of the troops are still discussed in the history of the war. The battle on the island was a turning point for American operations in the Pacific. The ceremony of the capture and the memory of the soldiers are still preserved in the United States and in Japan. The island has remained in history as a place of fierce battles, and the path of the Pacific soldiers is today material for educational programmes and museums.

analysis|02-20|1547|Ο Εδουάρδος ΣΤ΄ στέφεται βασιλιάς|Edward VI is crowned king|In the mid-sixteenth century England was in a period of intense religious and political change after the break with Rome. Henry VIII had died in 1547, leaving as heir his son Edward, who was still a child. Government would pass to a council of persons who would exercise power in his name. // On 20 February 1547 Edward was crowned king at Westminster, at the age of nine. The ceremony underlined the continuity of royal authority, although real political life was shaped by the councillors and by the factions of the court. The king's young age made authority fragile. // Edward's reign was short, as he died in 1553 at the age of fifteen. This period brought further religious reforms, but also fierce disputes over the succession. The coronation of 1547 is regarded as the beginning of a period in which political power was often concentrated in a few hands. The coronation of the young king was symbolic of the continuity of the monarchy. His era was important for the religious policy of England, and his history is still discussed by historians. His reign was linked with disputes over faith and the power of the court, and the sources of the period show intense political rivalry around the throne.

analysis|02-20|1909|Το Μανιφέστο του Φουτουρισμού στη Le Figaro|The Futurist Manifesto in Le Figaro|At the beginning of the twentieth century Europe was experiencing intense artistic searching, with new movements that challenged the traditional forms of art and literature. Speed, industry and technology seemed to be changing the way people lived. In Italy the poet Filippo Tommaso Marinetti was one of the central figures of the new movement. // On 20 February 1909 Marinetti published in the French newspaper Le Figaro the Futurist Manifesto, a text that called for a break with the past and for the glorification of speed, violence and the machine. The publication provoked a great debate in the artistic circles of Europe. // The manifesto gave rise to the Italian Futurist movement, which influenced painting, literature, architecture and music. Its ideas were later connected with broader political debates, and the movement is still questioned for its contacts with fascism. Its history remains important for the study of the avant-garde trends of the period. This manifesto became the occasion for artistic controversies across Europe. Its influence can be seen in the painting, literature and architecture of the early twentieth century.

analysis|02-20|1962|Ο Τζον Γκλεν γίνεται ο πρώτος Αμερικανός σε τροχιά γύρω από τη Γη|John Glenn becomes the first American in orbit around the Earth|At the beginning of the 1960s the space race between the United States and the Soviet Union was at its height. The Soviet Union had already sent Gagarin into space, and the Americans were trying to make up the lost ground. The Mercury mission was the first crewed programme of the United States, with the aim of testing the human ability to live in orbit. // On 20 February 1962 the astronaut John Glenn was launched in the spacecraft Friendship 7 and completed three orbits around the Earth. The flight lasted almost five hours, and the spacecraft's systems worked with considerable success. This achievement moved the American public. // Glenn's flight strengthened the position of the United States in the space race and opened the way to the following programmes, such as Gemini and Apollo. The act is regarded as an important step in the development of crewed flight. Glenn's story remains one of the best-known chapters of American space history. The flight contributed to public confidence in crewed programmes. Scientists of the time used its data to improve future space systems.

analysis|02-21|1848|Δημοσιεύεται το «Κομμουνιστικό Μανιφέστο»|The Communist Manifesto is published|In the mid-nineteenth century Europe was experiencing industrialisation, the growth of the industrial proletariat and the social tensions that accompanied the development of the cities. At that time many revolutionary movements broke out in various countries, with demands for democracy and social justice. In London a circle of exiled political activists was seeking a common ideological formulation. // On 21 February 1848 the "Communist Manifesto" by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels was published in London, a short text that described the history of societies as a history of class struggles. The work called on workers to organise and to claim power, in a clear and forceful language. The publication was small at first, but its influence grew quickly. // The Manifesto became one of the most important political texts of the modern era, with influence on movements, parties and governments all over the world. Its ideas were questioned and revised many times, and historians still discuss its consequences for the twentieth century. Its significance is twofold: as a text of its own time and as a source for understanding the political developments that followed. The text was translated into many languages and became a basic point of reference for the labour movements. Its ideas were linked with many political developments of the twentieth century.

analysis|02-21|1916|Αρχίζει η μάχη του Βερντέν|The Battle of Verdun begins|At the beginning of the First World War the front in Western Europe had settled into trenches, and the military commands were looking for decisive attacks. Verdun, an old French fortress, had symbolic and strategic importance for the French defence. The German commander Falkenhayn planned an attack aimed at wearing down the French forces. // On 21 February 1916 German forces opened heavy artillery fire on the French positions around Verdun, and the battle began with great intensity. The fighting lasted almost ten months, with huge losses on both sides. The area was turned into a field of destruction, with trenches and ruins. // Verdun has remained in history as a symbol of the horror of war and of the endurance of the French troops. The battle contributed to the exhaustion of both sides, with no clear winner in the end. The battlefields are preserved today as memorials, and the memory of the battle is still discussed as an example of the human tragedy of war. This battle became a symbol of the endurance of the French troops, and the defence of Verdun remains in French memory. The battlefields are accessible to visitors today. This battle contributed to shaping the political debate on the sacrifices of war, and historians still study it.

analysis|02-21|1919|Δολοφονείται ο Κουρτ Άισνερ|Kurt Eisner is assassinated|After the First World War Germany was in deep crisis, with the collapse of the empire and fierce political clashes between socialists, liberals and conservatives. Bavaria had been declared a state, and Kurt Eisner, a socialist, took over as its prime minister. His government faced many difficulties in the economy and in social calm. // On 21 February 1919 Eisner was assassinated in Munich by a young nationalist officer, as he was on his way to the parliament. The murder caused unrest and was followed by the proclamation of the Bavarian Soviet Republic, a short-lived government with a revolutionary character. // This murder showed the intensity of German political life after the war and the vulnerability of democratic institutions. The short-lived Soviet republic was suppressed afterwards, and the event is regarded as a forerunner of the political polarisation that followed in Germany. Eisner's memory remains a point of reference in the history of Bavaria. Eisner's death opened a period of political instability in Bavaria. The contradictions of the era are reflected in the archives of the city of Munich. The period was full of contradictions, with society seeking stability and political life moving between hope and violence, as the texts of the time testify.

analysis|02-21|1965|Δολοφονείται ο Μάλκολμ Χ|Malcolm X is assassinated|At the beginning of the 1960s the civil rights movement of African Americans in the United States was in a phase of intense confrontation, with different strategies between non-violent and more radical tendencies. Malcolm X was one of the best-known representatives of the second tendency, and his rhetoric provoked debate. He had previously left the religious organisation that had made him known. // On 21 February 1965 Malcolm X was assassinated while speaking in a hall in New York, at an event of his organisation. The killer fired in the midst of the audience, and the slaughter shocked public opinion. The murder became one of the best-known crimes associated with the history of civil rights. // His death left deep marks on the movement, and his figure is still discussed with different interpretations. His later autobiography contributed to shaping his image, and his legacy influenced many generations of activists. The case remains part of the wider history of racial justice in the United States. His murder was a severe blow to the movement and provoked discussion about violence and the security of leaders. His legacy continues to be discussed at many universities and museums.

analysis|02-21|1972|Ο Νίξον επισκέπτεται το Πεκίνο|Nixon visits Beijing|In the early 1970s China and the United States had no diplomatic relations, since Beijing was outside the international recognition of Washington. The Soviet Union was a common concern, and the two countries began to consider ways of rapprochement. President Nixon wanted to change the geopolitical balance of the Cold War. // On 21 February 1972 Richard Nixon arrived in Beijing and met Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai. The visit was historic, since it was the first time an American president had travelled to China. The talks led to the signing of the Shanghai Communiqué, which set out the differences and the common ground between the two countries. // The visit changed relations between the two countries and affected the geopolitical balance of Asia and of the Cold War. This diplomatic move opened the way to the recognition of the People's Republic by the United States a few years later. The story of the journey remains an example of realpolitik. The visit changed the dynamics of relations between the two countries and the subsequent diplomatic moves. The image of the journey is preserved in history as a symbol of the new diplomacy.

analysis|02-21|1975|Καταδικάζονται στο σκάνδαλο Γουοτεργκέιτ|Convicted in the Watergate scandal|The Watergate scandal began in 1972 with the illegal entry into the offices of the Democratic Party in Washington, and developed into a major political crisis for the Nixon administration. Investigative journalistic revelations and congressional inquiries uncovered attempts to obstruct justice. The affair touched close associates of the president. // On 21 February 1975 former attorney general John Mitchell and two former White House advisers were sentenced to prison terms for their role in the affair. The decision was important, because it showed that even senior government officials could be held accountable before the law. // The affair led to Nixon's resignation in 1974 and changed the American perception of the transparency of power. The scandal is linked with new laws on the financing of campaigns and with stronger congressional oversight. It remains one of the most important lessons in American political history. The case strengthened the need for transparency in government and in electoral campaigns. The lessons of the affair are taught in law schools and political institutes. The subject has returned to public debate many times, and the relationship between politicians and campaign finance remains an issue for every democracy.

analysis|02-22|1632|Ο «Διάλογος» του Γαλιλαίου|Galileo's "Dialogue"|At the beginning of the seventeenth century the scientific debate on the motion of the planets and the position of the Earth was intense, with the theory of Copernicus winning followers among scholars. The Catholic Church, which had already criticised these views, was wary of any public discussion that supported them. Galileo was trying to present his arguments clearly. // In 1632 Galileo published in Florence the "Dialogue on the Two Chief World Systems", a work written in the form of a conversation among three speakers. The publication had received the approval of the censors, but the text was regarded by theologians as defending the Copernican theory. The reaction was immediate and fierce. // The "Dialogue" led Galileo to trial by the Inquisition and to his condemnation to house arrest. The work remains as a landmark of scientific thought and of the conflict between science and ecclesiastical authority. Its importance lies in the form of the dialogue and in the free exchange of ideas. The Dialogue contributed to the spread of Copernicus's ideas in Europe. Reading it today shows the power of argument in science.

analysis|02-22|1732|Γεννιέται ο Τζορτζ Ουάσινγκτον|George Washington is born|At the beginning of the eighteenth century colonial Virginia was an area of tobacco plantations, an agrarian economy and sharp social division, where land and enslaved labour determined the prosperity of families. The Washington family belonged to the local landowners and had access to the public life of the colony. Education for the young was limited, but in some families it was relatively good. // On 22 February 1732 George Washington was born in Virginia, on a plantation near the Potomac River. In his youth he studied geometry, geodesy and land management, which gave him practical experience. His early life was linked with military service during the colonial conflict with France. // Washington later became the first president of the United States and leader of the Revolutionary War, and his life is regarded as central to the birth of the American state. His figure remains a point of reference for democracy, for virtue in power and for stepping down after two terms. His birth is linked with an era that was changing the world. His birth is linked with the biography of a man who became a national leader. His biographers examine the early years of his life in Virginia.

analysis|02-22|1879|Ανοίγει το πρώτο κατάστημα Woolworth|The first Woolworth store opens|At the end of the nineteenth century retail trade in the United States was growing rapidly, but most shops sold at high prices and with limited variety. Cities were growing, and the urban population wanted cheap and everyday products. A new way of retailing began to emerge, with low and stable prices. // On 22 February 1879 the first store of the Woolworth chain, founded by Frank Woolworth, opened in Utica, New York. The store sold goods at low prices, and the idea of a fixed price was then pioneering. Woolworth sought ways to keep costs low and goods moving quickly. // The chain expanded rapidly, and its stores became known across the country, while its way of operating influenced the form of retail trade. Its success brought significant growth for decades. Today the name Woolworth recalls an era when trade became more accessible to consumers. This store opened the way for the chain model, which became common in the American market. Its success is recorded in many studies of economic history. Its success was linked with the growth of urban centres, where workers sought cheap everyday products without long distances to travel.

analysis|02-22|1943|Εκτελείται η Σοφί Σολ|Sophie Scholl is executed|In the years of the Second World War Nazi Germany had imposed a harsh regime, and resistance was limited. Sophie Scholl was a student in Munich, and together with her brother Hans and other students she had organised the activity of the "White Rose", which distributed leaflets against the regime. The texts called for moral resistance and freedom. // On 22 February 1943 Sophie Scholl, Hans Scholl and Christoph Probst were executed by beheading in Munich, a few days after their arrest. The trial was brief and the sentence was immediate, without much time being given for a defence. Sophie was only twenty-one years old. // The execution shocked the members of the group and those who knew their story, and her figure became a symbol of moral resistance. Today her memory is honoured with monuments and educational initiatives, and the leaflets of the White Rose are studied as texts of human dignity. Sophie remains a symbol of young people who resist oppression. Her intellectual work is studied in schools and museums in Germany. Her story is still taught in schools, and her letters are studied as a source for understanding the moral stance towards a totalitarian power.

analysis|02-22|1943|Εκτελούνται τα μέλη της Λευκής Ρόζας|Members of the White Rose are executed|The White Rose group consisted of students who wrote and distributed leaflets against Hitler, in a period when Nazi power was almost absolute. Their activity was limited in number but clear in its message. The group had scholars and students of Munich in its leadership. // On 22 February 1943 Sophie Scholl, her brother Hans and Christoph Probst were executed, having been convicted for distributing the leaflets. The execution was carried out by beheading, after a trial that lasted only a few hours. The three young people faced death with dignity, according to the testimonies of the time. // Their sacrifice became a symbol of moral resistance against totalitarianism, and their memory remains a basic part of the German debate on democracy. Their leaflets are studied in schools and universities, as evidence that conscience can resist power. Their story reminds us of the importance of personal responsibility in difficult times. The White Rose kept the character of moral resistance, without resorting to violence. Its story is still discussed at memorial events every year. In post-war Germany the memory of the group's members was linked with the effort to recognise the resistance of ordinary citizens and to teach it in schools.

analysis|02-22|1980|Το «Θαύμα στον Πάγο»|The "Miracle on Ice"|In the early 1980s the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union had reached sport too, and ice hockey was one of the events with the greatest symbolic significance. The Soviet team was regarded as the strongest in the world, with professional players, while the American team consisted mainly of amateurs and students. // On 22 February 1980, at the Lake Placid Winter Olympics, the American team defeated the Soviet Union 4-3 in a game that remained in history. The victory was regarded as unexpected and went beyond sport, since it was linked with the political climate of the time. The emotion of the public was great. // The "Miracle on Ice" remains one of the best-known episodes in Olympic history, and the image of the team is still referred to in films and books. The victory boosted American morale in a difficult period and is a symbol of the unpredictable power of sport. Its story is still taught as an example of collective effort. The game was broadcast on television and moved audiences across America. The victory was linked with the memory of the era and with the confrontation between the two superpowers.

analysis|02-22|1997|Ανακοινώνεται η Ντόλι|Dolly is announced|At the end of the twentieth century biology was in an era of rapid developments, with molecular research and genetic techniques opening new paths. Cloning had until then been regarded as possible only in mammalian embryos, and scientists were looking for ways to use adult cells. The issue was scientifically difficult and ethically contested. // Researchers at the Roslin Institute in Scotland announced on 22 February 1997 that they had cloned the sheep Dolly, the first mammal to be created from the cell of an adult animal. The success was based on the transfer of the nucleus of a body cell into an egg cell, and the animal was born normally. The news aroused worldwide interest. // Dolly became a symbol of biotechnology and opened the debate on the ethics of cloning and on the limits of scientific intervention. Her success affected research in many fields, from medicine to agriculture. Today her case is cited as a milestone in the history of biology. The announcement was widely discussed in matters of the ethics of biotechnology. Dolly's story was linked with cloning legislation in many countries. This announcement changed the way scientists think about cells and about the development of organisms, and opened new fields of research.

analysis|02-23|1898|Καταδικάζεται ο Εμίλ Ζολά|Émile Zola is convicted|At the end of the nineteenth century France was divided by the Dreyfus affair, concerning a Jewish officer who had been convicted of espionage on the basis of disputed evidence. Antisemitic tendencies and the military world supported the conviction, while other intellectuals demanded a new inquiry. The dispute had taken over the press and political life. // In 1898 the writer Émile Zola published the open letter "J'accuse", addressed to the President of the Republic and accusing the military of a frame-up. On 23 February 1898 he was tried for libel and sentenced to imprisonment and a fine, and he was obliged to flee to England. His trial attracted great publicity. // Zola's action helped in the end to bring about a review of the Dreyfus trial and his later rehabilitation, and the letter became a model for the public protest of intellectuals. The term "intellectual" acquired at that time its present meaning. Zola's story remains one of the most important examples of freedom of expression in the West. The Zola affair left questions about the responsibility of journalists and intellectuals. "J'accuse" is still studied as a model of political writing. The case became a point of reference for freedom of the press and for the responsibility of institutions towards the truth.

analysis|02-23|1903|Η Κούβα νοικιάζει στις ΗΠΑ τον κόλπο του Γκουαντάναμο|Cuba leases Guantanamo Bay to the United States|After the war of 1898 Cuba was under American occupation, while the United States sought to keep strategic points in the Caribbean. Cuba formally gained independence, but American interventions were frequent. The naval presence in the region was regarded as necessary for protecting American interests. // On 23 February 1903 an agreement was signed under which Cuba leased Guantanamo Bay to the United States for use as a naval base. The lease was foreseen to last indefinitely, in exchange for an annual sum. The agreement gave the Americans a port of lasting importance on the island. // The base remains in operation to this day, and it has later been linked with debates about American interventions and about human rights. Its existence is a source of tension in relations between Cuba and the United States, since Cuba considers that the agreement is incompatible with its national sovereignty. This case has become a symbol of colonial legacy in the region.
